body_markdown:
Today’s performance SUVs are polished, calculated things. They are engineered to within an inch of their lives, assembled on shared platforms, and sold in vast numbers to people who will never take them anywhere more challenging than a damp Aldi parking lot.


I know this as a recent convert; not long ago, my wife bought a Maserati Levante with the twin-turbo V-6. They are staggeringly capable, deeply impressive, and about as rebellious as a quarterly earnings report. Yet there are few things I’d rather slink home in from a rainy late-night landing at Heathrow. The very first performance SUV, however, was very different.


The Lamborghini LM002 does not so much ignore convention as actively insult it. It is excessive in every measurable dimension, a machine conceived with the kind of decision-making process that suggests nobody in the room ever said the word “no.” Its “Rambo Lambo” nickname feels less like marketing and more like a warning.


The LM002’s backstory only reinforces the sense that this should never have happened. In the late 1970s, Lamborghini set its sights on a U.S. military contract, producing the Cheetah, a rear-engined off-road prototype powered by a Chrysler V-8. The layout was fundamentally flawed, the handling unpredictable, and the military looked elsewhere. That, by any reasonable standard, should have been the end of the matter.


Wiki Commons


Lamborghini


Lamborghini


Lamborghini


Instead, Lamborghini treated failure as a starting point. The concept was reworked, the engine moved to the front, and the target market shifted from the Pentagon to oil wealth and aristocratic curiosity. Then came the masterstroke of insanity: Rather than install something sensible, the Italians reached into their own catalog and selected a version of the[Countach](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=lamborghini+countach) V-12.


The result is a vehicle that appears less designed than imposed upon reality. It has all the visual subtlety of heavy machinery. Vast planes of aluminum and fiberglass form a shape that prioritizes intimidation—just the thing for despots the world over (Libyan dictator Muammar Gaddafi apparently ordered three for himself). The Lambo’s hood bulges to accommodate the intake system, while beneath each corner sit enormous Pirelli Scorpion tires, developed specifically for this application and capable of dealing with terrain that would defeat most vehicles outright.


Broad Arrow


Broad Arrow


Climbing aboard feels like mounting a piece of industrial equipment. Once inside, the contrast is almost comical. The underlying structure is upright and functional, yet it is smothered in leather, wood, and thick carpeting. The transmission tunnel rises through the cabin like a geological feature, dividing occupants into their own padded territories. Switches are scattered with little apparent logic, but by this point you are no longer expecting coherence.


Turn the key and any remaining sense of normality disappears. The 444-horsepower 5.2-liter V-12, closely related to the unit found in the Countach and fed by six Weber carburetors, does not settle into a polite idle. It chatters, barks, and fizzes with mechanical intent. There is nothing relaxed about it. You’re certainly awake.


Broad Arrow


Broad Arrow


Broad Arrow


Broad Arrow


Apply throttle and the entire vehicle seems to gather itself before surging forward. Induction noise builds into a deep roar, the exhaust hardens into a metallic howl, and this enormous mass accelerates with a conviction that feels faintly absurd. It is not graceful, but it is undeniably effective.


Everything about the driving experience demands effort. The clutch is heavy, the manual gearbox requires commitment, and the steering, though assisted, offers more resistance than finesse. Body movement is constant, reminding you that this is a very large object attempting to behave like something much smaller. Yet, for all that, the 6000-pound LM002 was capable of reaching 60 mph in roughly 8 seconds and continuing to speeds that feel entirely inappropriate for something of this scale.


The costs of such indulgence are as dramatic as the concept itself. Fuel consumption borders on the theatrical, necessitating fuel tanks totaling 77 gallons (inconveniently located in the cabin, beneath the rear seats) simply to make the car usable. Braking performance is constantly working against mass and momentum, and every journey carries a sense of mechanical expenditure.


If the Lamborghini LM002 itself was an exercise in excess, then its clientele followed suit. This was never a car for the merely wealthy. In an era before superyachts, it was for those who had already exhausted the obvious ways of demonstrating financial dominance and were now searching for something more theatrical. The typical buyer was not interested in subtlety or restraint. They wanted presence, spectacle, and a machine that made absolutely no attempt to justify itself.


Unsurprisingly, much of the Lamborghini LM002’s early life was spent in the Middle East, where its combination of off-road capability and operatic engine note made a certain kind of sense. Here was a vehicle that could cross desert terrain at speed while announcing its arrival from several miles away. It became a favorite among oil magnates and royal families, often specified in colors and trims that made even Lamborghini’s standard palette look conservative.


Broad Arrow


Elsewhere, the LM002 attracted a different but equally committed audience. European aristocrats, collectors, and a handful of celebrities found themselves drawn to its sheer improbability. It was less a rational purchase and more an acquisition, something to be added to a collection that already contained everything else.


There were, of course, attempts to push the concept even further. Special orders appeared, including the wagon-style LM002 variants, and there are rumors of even more outlandish specifications commissioned by particularly enthusiastic clients. Each one reinforced the same basic idea: This was not a vehicle shaped by market demand. It was shaped by the desires of a very small group of people who could afford to ignore such constraints entirely.


This 1989 LM002 wagon was custom built for Hassanal Bolkiah, the Sultan of Brunei.


Wikimedia Commons/Detectandpreserve


Lamborghini built just 301 LM002s between 1986 and 1993 (some sources cite 328), including 48 LM/American models specifically developed for U.S. export. They differ from their earlier counterparts by employing fuel injection cribbed from the[Diablo](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=lamborghini+diablo) , along with upgraded interiors, more chrome trim, and relocated fuel tanks.


Given their low production and wide dispersion, the market for LM002s is rather small. But with the rise of Lamborghini as a brand in the collector world, along with the rise of vintage trucks and SUVs as well as ’80s vehicles in general, LM002 prices have unsurprisingly been on an upward trajectory. In the early 2010s, nice examples hovered around $100,000. They increased sharply in 2015, then rose steadily for years but have been largely flat for the last 12 months.


Depending on model year, condition #3 (good) values currently range from $263,000 to $336,000, while condition #2 (excellent) values range from $328,000 to $377,000. Several exceptional examples have crossed the $400,000 mark, and the current record is a[$703,500](https://rmsothebys.com/auctions/mo24/lots/r0092-1989-lamborghini-lm002/#/utm_source=rss&utm_medium=classified&utm_campaign=MO24) sale from 2024.


[Today’s Lamborghini SUV](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/lamborghini-urus-and-lm002-are-suvs-worlds-apart/) , the Urus, is faster, more capable, and infinitely more sophisticated. It is also the product of committees, regulations, and shared engineering logic. The Lamborghini LM002 belongs to an era when none of that seemed especially important.


What remains is a monument to excess in its purest form. The LM002 is loud, demanding, inefficient, and completely unreasonable. It is also unforgettable. A machine born from a failed military idea and elevated, against all sensible judgement, by the addition of a V-12 from Sant’Agata Bolognese.
